# Native display border width controls

Original fixtures generated by tools/border_device_pixels_fixture.py, containing
six one-cell tables with single blue borders of 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 16 eighth-points.
Two sources distinguish compatibility modes 14 and 15. Arial is referenced, not
bundled. Both sources pass sixteen XML schema checks in total.

The reference application was observed directly through Windows Computer Use,
after the reference-opening helper confirmed each exact file was open. The reference application view showed
100% or 200% zoom. At 100%, the 8.5-inch page spans 816 display pixels (96 DPI).
Screenshot JPEGs were decoded only to measure text-free interior columns; a
border row requires all RGB channels below 210. screen-observations.json records
the scan positions and contiguous row ranges, bound to the exact source hashes.
These are live reference application observations, not measurements of a rasterized PDF.

At 100%, both compatibility modes paint the six widths as 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2 pixels.
At 200%, the first four mode-14 widths paint as 1, 1, 2, 2 pixels. The remaining
two controls were below the visible viewport. These observations are consistent
with flooring the device-pixel width, with a one-pixel minimum. They do not yet
prove all zoom boundaries, coordinate phases, joins or clipping behavior.

native-15.pdf preserves native document geometry independently of display rounding.
browser-baseline.json measures the current painter at scales 1 and 2 on transparent
canvases. The 0.25pt border at scale 1 has approximately 0.329 pixel-equivalent alpha
coverage, versus the reference application's single dark row. Thus changing the imported OOXML width
would be the wrong layer: the pending fix concerns display painting.

Run `node tools/measure-border-device-pixels.mjs` with Vite on port 5173 to repeat
the browser measurements. This is a diagnostic, not a passing fidelity test.
The manifest hashes the original sources and evidence. This initial evidence
commit did not change production painting: corner joins, clipped cells and
shading intersections first needed consistent treatment.

An independent-stroke rounding candidate was subsequently rejected. The 1pt
control at scale 2 exposes the problem: a horizontal origin at approximately
154 CSS pixels and thickness 4/3 CSS pixels paints device rows 308–309 when
thickness is floored, but rounding the adjoining vertical inner endpoint puts
its first row at 311. The six frames yielded eight opaque connected components.
Straight-width matching alone is therefore insufficient. Keep the connected
frame requirement alongside the measured widths, and verify mixed border joins
and clipped/shaded intersections before accepting a replacement painter.

The replacement table painter now retains relative logical junctions and rebuilds
corners, crossings and hidden merge caps after device-width rounding. Authored
thickness still decides crossing ownership when unequal widths round equally.
The native-width tests also check six connected frames at both scales and an
editor edit/undo/export/reopen cycle. The fractional primitive remains available
unchanged for paragraph and other geometric painting.

construction-screen.json records a separate native regression check: all three
changed Construction brochure rules paint as three pixels in the live reference application at 100%.
The new browser painter matches that thickness; its surrounding page pixels and
document layout remain unchanged. These observations do not certify all zoom
phases, rotated contexts, or device rasterization of non-single border patterns.

bistro-screen.json records the same distinction on corpus source #229. Its
0.25pt rule is one dark display pixel in the live reference application at 100%, matching the app;
a lighter fractional-width PDF raster is not evidence of a display mismatch.
The native screenshot is retained in scratch with its hash in the record.
